item.title: One-Step Self-Assembling Lipopolymer Coatings Enable Direct Longitudinal Biosensing in Native Biological Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2611.27422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sample-driven cross-reactivity remains a fundamental bottleneck for sensitive and selective biosensing in complex biological environments, particularly in microfluidic systems where high surface-to-volumes ratios amplify non-specific interactions. Here, we address this challenge with a one-step, biomimetic surface functionalization strategy based on engineered lipid-based nanocarriers that self-assemble within minutes into immunoassay-ready, antifouling interfaces that couple pegylated-lipid passivation with biorthogonal, site-specific probe conjugation. This approach enables rapid, tuneable, and reproducible surface functionalization, which suppresses sample-specific cross-reactivity even in undiluted serum, and supports direct, label-free digital biosensing assays directly in native biological environments. When integrated into an optofluidic platform combining digital in-line holography and microfluidics, this approach allows time-resolved quantification of tetraspanin-positive extracellular vesicle secretion dynamics from two-dimensional and three-dimensional lung cancer cell models using 50 {\mu}L of sample within 10 min, without isolation or purification. Because the presented surface functionalization proceeds via self-assembly rather than covalent surface modification, this one-step modular-approach is intrinsically decoupled from device fabrication and applies to both glass and PDMS, coating the entire microfluidic channel, thereby establishing a general route for integrating biomimetic nanostructures into robust, high-performance immunoassays, advancing biosensing beyond end-point measurements, and towards rapid and continuous real-time monitoring.
item.dc:creator: Pascal R\"uedi, Sarina Seiter, Stephan Handschin, Chiara Lombardo, Jaime Ortega Arroyo, Romain Quidant

item.title: MambaSplit: Severity-Robust and Inference-Efficient Semantic Unmixing of Fluorescence Microscopy Image Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.26703v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The number of structures fluorescence microscopy can image in one sample is limited by how few fluorophores can be separated without significant spectral overlap. Semantic unmixing circumvents this limit by imaging two structures in one fluorescent channel and computationally separating the superimposed image into one image per structure. Because pixels rarely identify their structure, unmixing requires both local and long-range spatial context. The relative brightness of the two structures is unknown and can be very uneven, so predictions must remain accurate across mixing severities, from balanced mixtures to ones where a structure is barely visible. Existing methods either process small image patches or add context through auxiliary pathways that slow inference on large images. We present MambaSplit, a hierarchical state-space encoder with a convolutional decoder that captures context across large tiles in linear time and predicts both channels in one deterministic pass. MambaSplit trains either on computationally summed channel images with random mixing ratios, where a lightweight head estimates the unknown ratio and conditions the decoder on it, or on experimentally acquired superpositions. Across five datasets and nine mixing ratios, MambaSplit achieves the highest RI-PSNR, by up to 3.0 dB, in 11 of 15 dataset-severity combinations and ties in one more, while running 5.9x faster than the strongest baseline. On acquired superpositions, fine-tuning a model pretrained on summed inputs matches or exceeds all baselines. Ablations show that accuracy and robustness come mainly from the training recipe: large tiles, mixing ratios sampled across their full range (up to 11 dB over fixed-ratio training), and independently drawn channel crops (3.9 dB on BioSR). The state-space backbone makes large tiles affordable, enabling high-content screening and event-driven smart microscopy.

item.title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
item.description: arXiv:2611.26794v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).
item.dc:creator: Yixuan Duan, Kexin Geng, Hanwen Xu, Wei Qiu

item.title: Learning effective stochastic predator and prey dynamics across physical and biological systems from limited data
item.description: arXiv:2611.27405v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Constructing an effective low-dimensional stochastic model from sparse observations requires separating deterministic drift from state-dependent fluctuations when the governing interaction law is unknown. We formulate an adaptive neural stochastic differential equation with topology constraints (TC-AdaNSDE) for two-variable predator--prey dynamics. To regularize the inverse problem when data are scarce, the model combines flexible drift and correlated diffusion fields with density-adaptive local Kramers--Moyal moment estimates and soft phase-space constraints reflecting boundary saddle behavior near extinction and local stability near coexistence. Using a known nonlinear stochastic system, we first show that short-time trajectory error cannot assess diffusion accuracy on its own and must be paired with distributional measures of one-step transitions and long-time phase-space occupancy. We then apply this framework to macroscopic turbulence and zonal flow energies reduced from Hasegawa--Wakatani plasma simulations and to short ecological time series. In the sparse-data regime, TC-AdaNSDE reproduces both short-horizon evolution and long-time invariant energy distributions where deterministic reductions collapse and unconstrained stochastic fits diverge, while recovering physically interpretable drift and fluctuation fields across both physical and biological systems.
item.dc:creator: J. C. Huang, Z. S. Qu, R. Varennes, X. Garbet, C. G. Wang, C. Guet, D. Niyato, K. Lim, V. Grandgirard

item.title: Saddle Buckling of a Multicellular Alga Driven by Differential Growth
item.description: arXiv:2611.27563v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: During development of many simple multicellular organisms there is a complex interplay between cell growth and generation of an extracellular matrix that confers structure. We study this problem quantitatively using $Gonium~pectorale$, a 16-cell alga that transforms from a flat to a buckled shape during growth without cell division or rearrangement. Cell-level measurements and 3D reconstructions show that the $12$ peripheral cells grow faster than the central $4$, producing hoop stress that selects the saddle mode, whose amplitude displays a continuous bifurcation with classical square root singularity. These results are consistent with a continuum model of differential growth within F\"oppl--von K\'arm\'an theory, which yields information on the mechanical properties of the ECM. Implications of this transformation in evolutionary transitions to multicellularity are discussed.
item.dc:creator: Zhao Wang, Sumit Kumar Birwa, Jane Y. Y. Chui, Kyriacos Leptos, Raymond E. Goldstein

item.title: Critical slowing down in hive temperature does not provide actionable early warnings of honey bee colony collapse
item.description: arXiv:2611.27766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Early warning signals (EWS) based on critical slowing down (CSD) have been proposed as model-independent indicators of approaching ecological regime shifts and may help anticipate honeybee colony collapse. However, whether theoretically expected signals can be reliably observed and provide useful prediction in real-world systems remains uncertain. Here, we combine structural analysis, mechanistic modeling and longitudinal observations to assess the dynamical plausibility, detectability and predictive accuracy of CSD-based EWS for honeybee colony collapse. Our results show that the presence of EWS is not equivalent to successful prediction of the transition. The analyzed models exhibit regime shifts accompanied by CSD, but detecting these signals in finite and noisy observations requires longer and more densely sampled time series than typically available for practical monitoring. Moreover, in empirical temperature records, CSD-like trends were detectable but provided limited discrimination between colonies that subsequently collapsed and those that survived. Declining mean temperature provided slightly greater discrimination than conventional CSD indicators, although its predictive value remained modest. Non-Gaussian correlated noise and the imperfect correspondence between hive temperature and colony strength further constrained EWS performance. These findings show that EWS can exist at the dynamical level without becoming useful predictors at the observational level, at least for our case study, thus cautioning against treating CSD-based indicators as generic predictors of ecological collapse.
item.dc:creator: Daniele Proverbio, Els Weinans, Davide Frizzera, Desiderato Annoscia, Francesco Nazzi, Giulia Giordano

item.title: A Categorical Compositional Distributional Modelling for the Language of Life
item.description: arXiv:1902.09303v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Categorical Compositional Distributional (DisCoCat) model is a mathematical framework for computing the meaning of a sentence from the meanings of its words and the grammatical structure that combines them. Because biological sequences can be viewed as a "language of life", it is tempting to ask whether the DisCoCat model can also give insight into biological macromolecules. Here we take a first step in this direction for proteins, whose linguistic features are the most prominent among the macromolecules. We treat a protein as a sentence and its domains as words, take the biological function of a domain or protein as its meaning, and regard the arrangement of domains as the syntax. We give pregroup grammar types to protein domains and to the linker regions between them, show how type reductions are lifted to multilinear maps between vector spaces, and use these maps to compute a vector representation of a protein's function from vector representations of its domains. In particular, linkers act as relational "words" whose order-three tensors combine the two flanking domains into a vector in a single protein meaning space, so that the functions of proteins with different domain architectures can be compared by an inner product. We extend the construction to proteins with any number of domains, illustrate it with a numerical toy example and five Drosophila melanogaster proteins, discuss how the linker tensors could be learned and how the model could be tested, and relate it to protein language models and other developments since 2019.
item.dc:creator: Yanying Wu
